lesson_title: Count the World, Count Your Wish: The Counting Principle
hook_text: What are the chances a random 4-digit PIN has no repeated digit? Most people guess low. The real answer flips a coin.
clip_script: Your phone asks for a 4-digit PIN. How many are possible? Do not list them — draw four dashes, one per digit, ten options above each, and multiply: ten thousand. Now the interesting question: how many have all DIFFERENT digits? Same dashes, but the options shrink as digits get used up: 10, then 9, then 8, then 7. Multiply: five thousand and forty. So the probability a random PIN has no repeat is 5 040 over 10 000 — 0,504. Better than a coin flip. Repeats feel common; they are actually the minority. That is the whole topic in one move: count the world for the bottom, count your wish for the top, divide. Photos work the same way: six friends line up, 6 factorial, 720 line-ups. Two of them glued together? Five units times the swap inside the knot — 240. Chance they end up side by side at random: one third. Dashes, shrinking numbers, one clean fraction. No listing, ever.
visual_style: A glowing phone lock screen, four dashes filling with spinning digits, options counters ticking down from 10 to 7, then a class photo row with two friends snapping together on an elastic string.
mood: Quick-fingered, game-show energy, one genuinely surprising statistic.
pacing: Rapid dash-filling beats, a pause on the 0,504 reveal, playful bounce through the photo row finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and count anything without listing a single case.
